## Where we are

| Model | Determinism | Time | State |
|---|---|---|---|
| ODE (Day 1) | deterministic | continuous | continuous |
| Function map (Day 1) | deterministic | discrete | continuous |
| Markov chain (Day 1) | stochastic | discrete | discrete |
| **Jump process (now)** | **stochastic** | **continuous** | **discrete** |

All four are population models: the state is counts, not people.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes at the start of the day. These four axes are the map the whole
course is drawn on, and today fills in the last population-level corner:
stochastic, continuous in time, discrete in state. Point out that the
individual-level column is still empty; that is Day 3.
:::

## Why events matter

- A CTMC waits for the next infection or recovery.
- The state is integer-valued: $X=(S,I,R)$.
- Exact event timing exposes fade-out and peak variability.

For the baseline population,
$$
a_{\mathrm{inf}}=\frac{\beta cSI}{N},\qquad
a_{\mathrm{rec}}=\gamma I.
$$

::: {.notes}
Contrast this with an ODE: an ODE advances all flows over a numerical
interval, while a jump process samples the next event and its type.
:::

## Recap: where the exponential comes from

An event with constant hazard $r$ has waiting time $T$ with

$$
\Pr(T>t)=e^{-rt},\qquad \Pr(T\le\delta t)=1-e^{-r\delta t},
$$

the same conversion used for the discrete-time chain on Day 1.

::: {.notes}
Five minutes, no derivation on the board. Point out that the survival function
is where yesterday's rate-to-proportion rule came from: the per-step
probability is the chance the waiting time lands inside the step. The full
derivation is in the probability prerequisite; nobody needs to have read it to
follow this session.
:::

## Recap: memoryless clocks and which one rings first

Exponential waiting times are **memoryless**,

$$
\Pr(T>s+t\mid T>s)=e^{-rt}=\Pr(T>t),
$$

so no per-individual clock has to be carried and the counts $(S,I,R)$ are the
whole state. With competing events at rates $a_j$ and $a_0=\sum_j a_j$,

$$
\min_j T_j\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0),
\qquad \Pr(J=j)=\frac{a_j}{a_0}.
$$

::: {.notes}
Memorylessness is a real assumption about the disease: someone infectious for a
week is no closer to recovering than someone infected this morning. The two
displayed results are the whole Gillespie algorithm: when the next event
happens, and which one it is. The next slide is bookkeeping rather than new
mathematics. Learners who want the derivations should read the waiting-times
section of the probability prerequisite afterwards.
:::

## Gillespie direct algorithm

At state $x$, let $a_0=a_{\mathrm{inf}}+a_{\mathrm{rec}}$.

1. Draw $\tau\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0)$.
2. Choose infection with probability $a_{\mathrm{inf}}/a_0$.
3. Apply $(-1,+1,0)$ or $(0,-1,+1)$.

This is a stochastic, continuous-time, discrete-state, population-level
model.  Every event conserves $S+I+R=N$.

::: {.notes}
The propensities are rates, not probabilities.  The waiting time is continuous
even though the state changes by integer increments.
:::

## A visible Julia kernel {.smaller}

```{julia}
#| echo: true
using Random, StableRNGs

function gillespie_sir(N, I₀, β, c, γ, tmax, rng)
    t, x = 0.0, [N - I₀, I₀, 0]
    times, states = [t], [copy(x)]
    while t < tmax && x[2] > 0
        a = (β*c*x[1]*x[2]/N, γ*x[2])
        a₀ = sum(a)
        a₀ == 0 && break
        t += randexp(rng)/a₀
        t > tmax && break
        if rand(rng)*a₀ < a[1]
            x[1] -= 1; x[2] += 1
        else
            x[2] -= 1; x[3] += 1
        end
        push!(times, t); push!(states, copy(x))
    end
    (; times, states)
end
```

::: {.notes}
The state update is the stoichiometric change vector in code.  The local
StableRNG makes the result reproducible without relying on global state.
:::

## One path, and the ODE through it {.center .smaller}

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-slide-ch04-path
#| fig-cap: "One exact CTMC path (steps) against the mean-field ODE (dashed)."
using CairoMakie, OrdinaryDiffEq

path = gillespie_sir(1000, 10, 0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 40.0,
    StableRNG(20250711))
states = reduce(hcat, path.states)
@assert maximum(abs.(sum(states; dims=1) .- 1000)) == 0   # conservation

function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t)
    κ, γ = p
    du[1] = -κ*u[1]*u[2]
    du[2] =  κ*u[1]*u[2] - γ*u[2]
    du[3] =  γ*u[2]
end
grid = collect(0.0:0.2:40.0)
ode = Array(solve(ODEProblem(sir_drift!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0),
    (0.05*10/1000, 0.25)), Tsit5(); saveat = grid))

fig = Figure(size = (880, 320))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "people",
    title = "$(length(path.times)-1) events, peak I = $(maximum(states[2, :]))")
for (j, (name, col)) in enumerate(zip(["S", "I", "R"],
        [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen]))
    stairs!(ax, path.times, states[j, :]; color = col, linewidth = 2,
        label = "$name (jump)")
    lines!(ax, grid, ode[j, :]; color = col, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5)
end
axislegend(ax, position = :rc)
fig
```

::: {.notes}
This is the picture the whole morning is about. Every wiggle is a real event, and
at a thousand people there are well over a thousand of them, so the steps merge
into a rough curve. Zooming in on the first few days is where you would see
individual jumps. The dashed curves are yesterday's model, and the gap is not
solver error: this particular realization ran a few days late, and a
different seed would run early.

The title numbers are generated at render time and are realization-specific;
conservation is asserted, so a broken kernel would fail the render. Do not let
anyone read one path as an expected epidemic; that is the next two slides.
:::

## Recap: two kinds of spread

For $M$ independent paths with summary values $z_1,\dots,z_M$,

$$
\bar z=\frac1M\sum_k z_k,\qquad
s^2=\frac1{M-1}\sum_k (z_k-\bar z)^2,\qquad
\operatorname{se}(\bar z)=\frac{s}{\sqrt M}.
$$

- The standard deviation $s$ describes **the epidemics**: how much peak size
  varies. More simulation does not shrink it.
- The standard error $\operatorname{se}(\bar z)$ describes **our estimate** of
  the average, and does shrink, as $1/\sqrt M$: four times the work to halve it.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, and it pays for itself four times today. These two spreads get
confused constantly, so keep them apart: one is a property of the disease
process, the other a property of how hard we simulated. Say explicitly that this
is the vocabulary the rest of the day uses. The relative spread of SDE peaks
after the break, the variance-to-mean ratio of case counts this afternoon, and
the variance decomposition in the last session all live on this slide. Nobody
needs the probability prerequisite for it.
:::

## Three ways to write one model {.smaller}

The model has not changed since the last slide. Only the *notation* changes.

| | what you write | who writes the code |
|---|---|---|
| **Day 1** | a function: every term, by hand | you |
| **Today** | a macro: the model as stated | the library |

A hand-written function works in any language, and that is its virtue. It is
also longer than the mathematics it encodes, and every extra line is somewhere a
sign can go wrong. Macros let Julia read the model the way it is written on
paper and generate the loop for you — which is what makes a fifty-compartment
model tractable.

Two toolkits do this in SciML, and today uses both: **ModelingToolkit.jl** and
**Catalyst.jl**.

::: {.notes}
This is the framing slide for the rest of the day, so do not rush it. The point
is not that macros are clever; it is that all three representations are the same
process. The hand-written kernel earlier was deliberately the Day 1 style: it
could have been C or R, and you had to be the one who got the stoichiometry
right. Everything from here on states the model and lets the library write the
loop. Stress that this is a claim we are about to check, not a promise.
:::

## The ODE, by hand and by declaration {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Day 1: a kernel you write.

```{julia}
#| label: ch04-hand-ode
#| echo: true
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    κ, γ = p
    du[1] = -κ*S*I
    du[2] =  κ*S*I - γ*I
    du[3] =  γ*I
    return nothing
end
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Today: the equations, stated.

```{julia}
#| label: ch04-mtk-ode
#| echo: true
using ModelingToolkit
using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t,
                       D_nounits as D

@parameters κ γ
@variables S(t) I(t) R(t)

@named odesys = System(
    [D(S) ~ -κ*S*I,
     D(I) ~  κ*S*I - γ*I,
     D(R) ~  γ*I], t)
```
:::

::::

Three assignments into a `du` vector you must index correctly, against three
named equations. Day 1 wrote this with $\beta$, $c$ and $N$; here
$\kappa=\beta c/N$ throughout.

::: {.notes}
Put the two columns up and let them look before saying anything. The left is
exactly what we did yesterday and it is not bad code — it is fast, it is
explicit, and you could hand it to a C programmer. What it is not is the
mathematics: `du[2]` is the infectious equation only by a convention you have to
remember, and nothing stops you writing `du[1]` twice.

On the right `D(S) ~ -kappa*S*I` reads as the equation does, and the name `S`
travels with the model, which is why the solution object can answer `sol[S]`
later without you tracking that S was index one. The symbolic form is also what
lets the library differentiate the model, simplify it, or convert it to another
kind of process — none of which it can do with a function whose body it cannot
see. That is the trade: you give up nothing in speed, because the macro
generates a kernel like the one on the left.
:::

## The same model, two toolkits {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="54%"}
```{julia}
#| label: ch04-mtk
#| echo: true
using JumpProcesses

@named jumpsys = JumpSystem(
    [MassActionJump(κ, [S => 1, I => 1],
        [S => -1, I => 1]; scale_rates = false),
     MassActionJump(γ, [I => 1],
        [I => -1, R => 1]; scale_rates = false)],
    t, [S, I, R], [κ, γ])
```
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
```{julia}
#| label: ch04-catalyst
#| echo: true
using Catalyst

sir_network = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I --> 2I
    γ, I --> R
end
```
:::

::::

Who must be present sets the propensity; what the event does sets the state
change. Catalyst reads both off the arrow.

::: {.notes}
Read the two columns against each other rather than line by line. On the left
you say the two lists explicitly: `[S => 1, I => 1]` is why the propensity is a
product, `[S => -1, I => 1]` is the stoichiometric change vector. On the right
the arrow says both at once — that is the whole saving, and it is why a
reaction list stays readable at fifty reactions where a jump list does not.

One rate constant per transition, so the beta-c-S-I-over-N from this morning
becomes kappa-S-I with kappa equal to beta c over N. R nought is still 2. The
book chapter uses kappa from here on.
:::

## Equivalent, to the last event {.smaller}

```{julia}
#| label: ch04-equivalence
#| echo: true
using StableRNGs

start = [S => 990, I => 10, R => 0, κ => 0.05*10/1000, γ => 0.25]

mtk_path = solve(JumpProblem(complete(jumpsys), start, (0.0, 40.0);
                             rng = StableRNG(3001)), SSAStepper())

catalyst_path = solve(JumpProblem(sir_network,
                          [:S => 990, :I => 10, :R => 0], (0.0, 40.0),
                          [:κ => 0.05*10/1000, :γ => 0.25];
                          aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(3001)),
                      SSAStepper())

mtk_path(grid, idxs = I) == catalyst_path(grid, idxs = sir_network.I)
```

Not merely similar — given the same seed, the same sequence of events.

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that earns the word "equivalent". Both toolkits build the same
two mass-action jumps, hand them to the same Direct aggregator, and draw from
the same seeded stream, so the paths agree event for event, not just in
distribution. Lowered to ODEs instead, the two peaks agree to about 1e-16, which
is floating-point noise. If a comparison like this ever came out false you would
have found a real bug in one of the two descriptions, so it is worth running.
:::

## Which toolkit, and when? {.smaller}

| | ModelingToolkit.jl | Catalyst.jl |
|---|---|---|
| You describe | variables, equations, jumps | reactions |
| Stoichiometry | written out per jump | read off the arrow |
| Rate laws | any expression you write | mass action by default |
| Covers | ODEs, SDEs, jumps, DAEs, control | reaction networks |
| Comes with | structural simplification | network and conservation analysis |
| Reach for it when | the model is not a reaction network | it is |

Neither is a wrapper around the other, and neither is the "advanced" one. The
question is only whether your model is naturally a set of reactions.

::: {.notes}
The honest summary: if you can draw your model as arrows between boxes,
Catalyst will say it in fewer lines and give you network analysis for free.
Ageing, waning, vaccination schedules and contact matrices are all still
reactions, so that covers most of epidemiology. The moment you want a term that
is not a reaction — a delay, an optimal control, a mass-matrix constraint — you
are in ModelingToolkit, and Catalyst systems convert into it anyway.

Do not let anyone leave thinking they must pick one. The worksheet this
afternoon uses ModelingToolkit because jumps are the topic; the reaction
networks session later in the week is entirely Catalyst.
:::

## One `solve`, two processes {.smaller}

```{julia}
#| label: ch04-dispatch
#| echo: true
ode_problem  = ODEProblem(complete(odesys),   start, (0.0, 40.0))
jump_problem = JumpProblem(complete(jumpsys), start, (0.0, 40.0);
                           rng = StableRNG(3001))

ode_solution  = solve(ode_problem,  Tsit5())        # deterministic
jump_solution = solve(jump_problem, SSAStepper())   # one exact path

(ode = round(maximum(ode_solution[I]); digits = 1),
 jump = maximum(jump_solution[I]))
```

Different problem, different solver — but `solve`, `sol[I]` and `sol(grid)` are
the same words in both cases.

::: {.notes}
This is the multiple-dispatch argument, made concrete rather than asserted.
Everything that *differs* between a deterministic and a stochastic model is in
how the problem is built: differential equations against jumps, Tsit5 against
SSAStepper. Everything downstream is identical, because `solve` dispatches on
the problem type and the solution object answers `sol[I]` the same way whichever
process produced it. That is why the sensitivity, estimation and intervention
sessions later in the week can reuse one set of habits across model types
instead of learning a new interface each time. It is also why swapping a model
class is usually a two-line change, not a rewrite.
:::

## Twenty paths and the ODE {.center .smaller}

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-slide-ch04-ensemble
#| fig-cap: "Twenty CTMC paths of infectious prevalence with the mean-field ODE."
using Statistics

simulate_jump(seed) = solve(
    JumpProblem(complete(jumpsys), start, (0.0, 40.0); rng = StableRNG(seed)),
    SSAStepper())(grid, idxs = I)

M = 20
paths = [simulate_jump(3000 + k) for k in 1:M]
peaks = maximum.(paths)

fig2 = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax2 = Axis(fig2[1, 1], xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious",
    title = "peak I: mean $(round(Int, mean(peaks))), sd $(round(Int, std(peaks)))" *
            ", se $(round(std(peaks)/sqrt(M); digits = 1))")
for path in paths
    lines!(ax2, grid, path; color = (:firebrick, 0.35), linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(ax2, grid, ode[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2.5)
fig2
```

::: {.notes}
Five minutes, and let them look before you talk. Two things to point at. First
the spread in *timing*: every path has the same shape but peaks somewhere between
roughly day 12 and day 23. Second, and this is the one worth labouring: the
dashed ODE is not the average of the paths. Its peak is near 158 while the mean
of the twenty individual peak heights is around 178, because each path peaks at
its own time and averaging asynchronous peaks flattens the curve. So "the ODE
peak" and "the average peak of an epidemic" are different quantities.

The three numbers in the title are the previous slide made concrete: sd is the
epidemics varying, se is how well twenty runs pin the average down. Note that
none of these twenty paths fades out. With ten initial infectives and $R_0=2$
that is expected, since fade-out needs all ten introductions to fail. Fade-out is
a small-introduction phenomenon, and the worksheet quantifies it.
:::

## What exactness costs {.smaller}

Every event is simulated individually, so the work is set by the *event count*,
not by the time horizon. One counting kernel answers both questions:

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
function count_events(N, I₀, β, c, γ, tmax, rng; sis = false)
    t, S, I, n = 0.0, N - I₀, I₀, 0
    while t < tmax && I > 0
        infection = β*c*S*I/N
        a₀ = infection + γ*I
        t += randexp(rng)/a₀
        t > tmax && break
        if rand(rng)*a₀ < infection
            S -= 1; I += 1
        else
            I -= 1; sis && (S += 1)
        end
        n += 1
    end
    n
end
```

Timed over `N` from $10^3$ to $10^7$ with 1% initially infected, and — with
`sis = true`, so recovery returns to susceptible — over rising contact rates.

::: {.notes}
The kernel allocates nothing and is written the obvious way — no vectorisation,
no rewriting in C. That is the "Julia is fast" claim from this morning made
concrete: ten million events in a scalar loop is a reasonable thing to do here.
:::

## Cost grows with size and with rates {.center .smaller}

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-slide-ch05-cost
#| fig-cap: "Left: wall-clock time for one exact SIR path against population size, log-log, with a slope-one reference. Right: event count for an SIS model at N = 10⁵ as the contact rate rises."
count_events(1000, 10, 0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 40.0, StableRNG(1))       # warm up

sizes = [10^3, 10^4, 10^5, 10^6, 10^7]
cost = [@elapsed(count_events(N, N ÷ 100, 0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 40.0,
    StableRNG(1))) for N in sizes]

contacts = [5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0]
recycling = [count_events(10^5, 1000, 0.05, c, 0.25, 40.0,
    StableRNG(2); sis = true) for c in contacts]

reference = cost[1] .* sizes ./ sizes[1]

fig = Figure(size = (880, 320))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xscale = log10, yscale = log10,
    xlabel = "population size N", ylabel = "seconds per path",
    title = "one SIR path: cost ∝ N")
lines!(ax1, sizes, reference; color = :grey, linestyle = :dash,
    label = "slope 1")
scatterlines!(ax1, sizes, cost; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2,
    label = "measured")
axislegend(ax1; position = :lt)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "contact rate c", ylabel = "events per path",
    title = "SIS at N = 10⁵: reinfection lifts the 2N ceiling")
scatterlines!(ax2, contacts, recycling; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2)

fig
```

::: {.notes}
Two different reasons to be slow. Size is the obvious one: each individual is
moved through the system one event at a time, so the count comes out at about
1.55N here and the slope-one reference confirms the cost is linear in N.

Rates are the subtler one. In a closed SIR the event count can never exceed 2N,
because every individual is infected at most once — so raising the contact rate
only pushes you towards the final-size bound. Allow reinfection and that ceiling
goes: events then accumulate at roughly 2*gamma*I(t), so cost is driven by
endemic prevalence, which rises with the contact rate. Crossing the threshold
from c = 5 (R0 = 1) to c = 10 (R0 = 2) multiplies the work about thirty-fold.
It does not grow without limit, though: prevalence saturates towards N, so the
curve flattens off at roughly 2*gamma*N*tmax, which is 2e6 events here.

The honest summary is that exact simulation costs one step per event, and the
event count is what you have to reason about. That is where tau-leaping and
hybrid methods earn their place.
:::

## Takeaways

- Propensities determine both waiting times and event probabilities.
- Two notations, one process: ModelingToolkit and Catalyst give the same events.
- Exact jumps preserve integer states and population conservation.
- Ensemble summaries are needed for comparison with an ODE.
- Exactness is paid for per event, so cost follows the event count.

Invite readers to open the Pluto companion and change transmission or the
initial number infected.  The book contains the random time-change derivation
and exercises.
:::
